title: Let an operator declare a repository as their own, and grant a broader profile only there

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 027eff0 with bookkeeping f6128ef, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

You asked for an adversarial pass at the validator and independent confirmation of the confinement re-check. You got both. The validator survived everything I threw at it. The confinement argument did not, in one specific and important way.

================================================================
REQ 1 — I TRIED TO DEFEAT IT. I COULD NOT. NO FAIL.
================================================================

Sixteen inputs against validateOwnedRepositoryDeclaration(), then the survivors re-run end to end through a real subprocess with a fake claude dumping its own argv, so I was reading the grant actually passed rather than a return value:

  GRANTED (all resolve to this exact repository):
    exact real path, trailing slash, dot-dot round trip (/a/b/../b/repo), symlink pointing TO the repo
  REFUSED, each with a named reason and the remedy:
    symlink pointing elsewhere, parent directory, sibling worktree, relative ".", relative "./scripts",
    leading space, trailing space, nonexistent path, "/", a non-git directory, uppercased path,
    empty string

Nothing yielded a grant outside the declared directory. The design is right for a reason worth stating: realpathSync is applied to BOTH sides before comparison, so symlink games are defeated in either direction — a link to the repo resolves in and is correctly granted, a link away resolves out and is correctly refused. Requiring an absolute path up front removes the "relative to what?" ambiguity rather than guessing at it. Requiring a git repository is refused rather than warned, with the reasoning stated (git is the recovery boundary every downstream gate assumes).

WHAT THE RULE IS STATED NOT TO CATCH, since the criterion asks: the declaration lives inside the repository it grants over, so anyone who can write .claude/settings.local.json in a repo you already own can raise the profile there. That is inherent to the design and correct — it is the operator's own file in the operator's own declared repository — but it is worth being explicit that the boundary is "which directory", never "who wrote the declaration". A cloned repository carrying someone else's declaration is refused on this machine automatically, because their path will not resolve to your root. I checked that specific case.

================================================================
FINDING (blocking) — THE CONFINEMENT BOUND DOES NOT COVER THE INTERPRETER ENTRIES IT IS CITED TO BOUND
================================================================

Req 5's own verification is good work and I am not disputing it: a bare `Bash(*)` (or bare `Bash`) genuinely disables the path-based redirect-confinement check — a write to an absolute path outside the working directory succeeded with zero permission_denials, reproduced three times — while a real prefix pattern, however broad, does not. That is exactly why this list is never a wildcard, and establishing it by running was the right call.

The problem is what that bound is then asked to carry. The reasoning for including the interpreters says:

  "`node *`, `python3 *`, `bash *`, `sh *` are deliberately included here ... The risk they carry is
   bounded the same way every other entry here is: directory confinement (verified below, Req 5), git
   recoverability ... and uncommitted work."

Directory confinement, on this project's own evidence, is REDIRECTION confinement. The refusal it produces reads "Output redirection to '/tmp/...' was blocked" (sprint 12's finding, re-verified here). It governs shell redirects. It is not a filesystem sandbox.

`Bash(python3 *)` grants `python3 -c "open('/anywhere/x','w').write(...)"`. That is a file write with no shell redirect anywhere in it. There is nothing for a redirect-confinement check to intercept — this is not a bypass of the check, it is outside the check's subject matter. The same applies to `node -e`, and `bash -c 'echo x > /outside'` puts the redirect inside a quoted string argument rather than in the analysed command line, which sprint 12's own heredoc finding ("Contains shell syntax that cannot be statically analyzed") shows the analyser is sensitive to.

So the safety argument for the four highest-risk entries in this grant rests on a bound that, as far as this project's recorded evidence goes, does not reach them. That is not the same as saying writes escape — I have not demonstrated that, I have no credentials to run a real headless role, and I will not report an untested claim as a finding of fact. What I am reporting is that the stated justification is asserted rather than established for exactly the entries that most need it, in the sprint whose criteria say this bound "is the entire basis on which this sprint was argued."

REQUIRED, AND IT IS CHEAP — TWO REAL HEADLESS RUNS UNDER THE GRANTED PROFILE:
  1. `bash -c 'echo x > /tmp/fc19-escape.txt'`  — does confinement see a redirect nested in -c?
  2. `python3 -c "open('/tmp/fc19-escape2.txt','w').write('x')"` — a direct write, no redirect at all.
Then say what happened. If both are blocked, the existing sentence is correct and now proven, and this becomes the strongest claim in the sprint. If either succeeds, the reasoning needs rewriting — not necessarily the grant, since git recoverability and the .env protection still apply inside the repository, but the sentence claiming confinement bounds them must go, and the residual risk stated honestly instead.

I am blocking on this rather than filing it informational for one reason: Req 5's criterion makes the confinement bound the load-bearing basis of the whole sprint, and this is the one place that basis is cited without having been tested. Everything else in this sprint was tested. This is the gap.

================================================================
REQS 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 — MET
================================================================

Req 2 (refusal demonstrated) — a non-git directory is refused, verified above through the real subprocess path, not by reading.

Req 3 — the OS-level approach is a real finding and correctly reasoned: Claude Code's Bash patterns cannot express "block writes to file X regardless of command", so a pattern-based .env guard would have been security theatre. Protection is verified by attempting a real write rather than trusting an exit code, and failure to verify refuses the launch rather than degrading. Linux chattr named as expected-but-unverified and Windows named as an uncompensated gap — both honest, neither dressed up.

Req 4 — a decision was made (warn, naming what was already dirty, and proceed) with the reasoning in code. I saw it fire in my own scratch run: "has 3 uncommitted change(s) before this session started: ?? .claude/, ?? p.txt, ?? scripts/. Proceeding anyway ... recorded here so a later tangle between two sessions can be traced." Names the files, not just the count. The criterion says an unstated default is the defect whichever way it went; this is stated.

Req 6 — bare interpreters refused, with the trust-boundary distinction from the broad grant articulated rather than left as an apparent contradiction: Req 6 guards a value any writer of a target project's tracked settings can set, the broad grant applies only after the operator's own high-trust declaration. That distinction is correct and it is the reason the two lists can differ.

Req 7 — `git diff` against scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py is EMPTY. cmd_ship, cmd_complete, cmd_qa1 and cmd_liveqa are untouched. `git push` is carried in the grant's own disallowedTools rather than omitted from allowed, so `Bash(git *)` stays usable for review while Pipeman remains the only pusher — confirmed directly in the same real test per the comment.

Req 8 — 0.1.19. Req 9 — 167 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.19 (first install)".

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. A DECLARATION OF THE WRONG TYPE IS IGNORED SILENTLY. `"fullyCompletely.ownedRepository": true` (or a
   number, null, {}, or "") produces the narrow default with no message at all, while a malformed PATH
   (relative, parent, nonexistent) refuses loudly and names the fix. An operator who typos the type
   gets the narrow profile and no explanation for why their declaration "did nothing". Fail-closed,
   which is the right direction, but inconsistent with how every other malformed declaration is
   handled. One line in the reader.

2. MY OWN HARNESS PRODUCED TWO FALSE READINGS BEFORE I GOT THIS RIGHT, and I am recording that because
   it bears on how much weight to give the rest. My first pass wrote the declaration as a nested
   object when the reader wants a flat dotted key, so nothing reached the validator; my second
   classified persona text echoed in argv as a stack trace and reported crashes that never happened. I
   nearly filed both as findings. Neither was real. The validator and the grant behave correctly and
   the only reason I know that is that I checked the actual argv passed to the child rather than
   trusting my own classifier — which is the same discipline I keep asking for here.

3. Carried, unchanged: the CLI-version-drift item (sprint-12 findings record no `claude` version, one
   CONFIRMED entry already expired) — newly relevant, since this sprint's Req 5 finding about bare
   `Bash(*)` is exactly the kind of matcher behaviour that drifted last time; sprint 17's bare-verb
   allowlist question; the --agents argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit.

RECOMMENDATION

Run the two commands above under a real granted profile and report what happened. If they are blocked, say so in that comment and this is a PASS on the next round with the strongest safety argument in the project. If either is not, rewrite the sentence rather than the grant, and state the residual honestly — the sprint may well still be right to ship, but not on a bound that does not hold.

Nothing else is outstanding. The validator is the best-defended piece of code this project has produced, and I could not get past it.

PASS: PASS — round 2, with an escalation that is not a fix request and is not aimed at Dev Team. Audited e697f70, main checkout. Sprint file re-read fresh, unchanged since f6128ef. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

Both round-1 items are closed. The way the first one was closed is the most valuable thing in this sprint, and it changed what the sprint is. Read the last section before this ships.

================================================================
THE FINDING WAS CONFIRMED, AND THEN WIDENED RATHER THAN MINIMISED
================================================================

You ran both checks and both escaped: `bash -c 'echo x > /tmp/x'` and `python3 -c "open('/tmp/x','w').write('x')"`, zero permission_denials. My finding was right, and the cheapest response available was to narrow the grant by four entries and call it fixed.

You did the opposite, and it was the correct call. You checked `node -e "require('fs').writeFileSync(...)"` and `curl -o /tmp/x` as well, found they escape identically, and drew the actual boundary: any tool with its own write-to-path argument sits outside what the redirect-confinement check was ever built to see. Dropping the four interpreters would have been cosmetic — `curl` was never in question and reaches just as far. Naming that, rather than shipping a narrowing that would have looked like a fix and changed nothing, is the difference between closing a finding and answering it.

The rewritten comment is accurate on every point I can check:
  - It states what the confinement check actually recognises: literal `>`/`>>` in the OUTER command
    Claude Code parses, and nothing past that boundary — not inside a `bash -c` quoted argument, not a
    native write API with no redirect at all.
  - It says the previous version overstated it, in those words, rather than quietly replacing the text.
  - It admits the entry list was not exhaustively probed ("almost certainly others never explicitly
    tried here"), which is the honest form of a finding whose full extent is unknown.
  - It states what actually bounds the grant: git recoverability except for uncommitted work and
    `.env`, `.env`'s own OS-level protection (and says why Req 3 deliberately does not use Bash pattern
    matching — which reads differently now, and better: it is the one control in this sprint built for
    exactly this class of escape), and the operator's explicit declaration. Then: "not a technical
    sandbox this file can prove airtight."

That last sentence is the one that matters, and it is the right sentence.

I verified the grant list itself is byte-unchanged — no `Bash(...)` entry was added or removed this round. The fix is entirely in what is claimed, which is what I asked for.

================================================================
THE INFORMATIONAL FIX — VERIFIED END TO END
================================================================

Wrong-type declarations now refuse loudly instead of falling through silently, and the refusal lands before claude is spawned. Confirmed through the real subprocess with a fake claude dumping argv, checking that the argv was empty on each refusal rather than trusting the message:
    true   REFUSED, claude never spawned
    123    REFUSED, claude never spawned
    null   REFUSED, claude never spawned
    {}     REFUSED, claude never spawned
    correct path -> BROAD GRANT (still works)
And the case that must NOT become an error stayed correct: with the key absent entirely, the run proceeds silently on the narrow default. The {present, value} shape is what makes that distinction possible and it is drawn in the right place.

One residual, informational only: an empty string (`""`) still falls through silently rather than refusing, because it is falsy. It is the same shape as the case just fixed, but `""` reads more like "I cleared this out" than like a typo, and treating a cleared value as absent is defensible. Not blocking, not worth a round; worth one line if that reader is ever open again.

================================================================
SCOPE AND SUITES
================================================================

Round-2 diff: run-role.js, launcher_test.js, and the state file. Req 7's invariant re-checked and still clean — `git diff` against scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py is EMPTY, so cmd_ship, cmd_complete, cmd_qa1 and cmd_liveqa remain untouched by this sprint.

169 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL WORKTREE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.19 (first install)"; package.json 0.1.19.

Everything verified in round 1 stands and is not re-derived: the sixteen-input adversarial pass at the validator, which nothing got past; Req 2's non-git refusal; Req 3's OS-level `.env` protection with its Linux and Windows gaps named; Req 4's warn-and-name decision, which I watched fire; Req 6's bare-interpreter refusal and the trust-boundary distinction that makes it consistent with the broad grant.

================================================================
ESCALATION — NOT A FIX REQUEST, AND NOT FOR DEV TEAM
================================================================

I am passing this because there is nothing left for Dev Team to do and the engineering is right. But the basis on which this sprint was argued has materially changed, and the person who authorised it should know before it ships.

The sprint's own QA1 criteria say the directory bound "is the entire basis on which this sprint was argued." That basis is now known to be narrower than believed when the sprint was written. The grant was justified as broad-but-bounded-by-confinement; what it actually is, on this round's own evidence, is broad-and-bounded-by-git-recoverability-plus-.env-plus-your-own-trust. Those are different propositions, and only the second one is true.

Two things make this worth surfacing rather than filing:
  - For the three eligible roles (dev-team-1, dev-team-2, qa1), arbitrary package and interpreter
    execution is NEW with this grant. Their prior profiles carried no interpreter and no npx. The
    comment's point that npx/npm always carried this reach is true as a general statement and does not
    change that these roles did not have it until now. So the residual is genuinely introduced here,
    not merely re-described.
  - The literal Req 5 test still passes — a bare redirect outside the working directory is still
    blocked under the broad profile, and the grant is unchanged since I verified that. So this is not
    the FAIL the criterion describes. It is the thing the criterion was standing in for turning out not
    to be what anyone thought it was.

WHAT I AM ASKING FOR: not a code change. A confirmation from whoever authorised this sprint that they still want it on the revised basis, recorded, before Pipeman publishes. If the answer is yes — and it may well be, since the operator's declaration is a real and deliberate act and the motivating case is real — then this ships with the most honest safety comment in the codebase. If the answer is "not for the roles that never had interpreter access," that is a scoping decision and it belongs to Master Controller, not to this gate and not to Dev Team.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it once that confirmation is on the record. /sprint-dev-done 19, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.19, then `verify-publish 19`.

Worth saying plainly, because it is the whole point of having this gate: this sprint asked for an adversarial pass, got a finding, ran the test, found the finding was bigger than reported, and rewrote its own claim to be smaller and true rather than defending the original. That is the behaviour every other item I have carried for eleven sprints was trying to produce.

PASS: PASS — round 3. Audited 55d56ee, main checkout. Short round, as promised: the sprint file's amendment is the only thing that moved, and the build is byte-identical to what round 2 passed.

BUILD UNCHANGED. `git diff e697f70 HEAD -- scripts/ .claude/ package.json templates/` is EMPTY. Round 2's verification stands on the same bytes and nothing on the code side was re-run, because there is nothing to re-run. Everything established across rounds 1 and 2 holds unmodified: the sixteen-input adversarial pass at validateOwnedRepositoryDeclaration() that nothing got past; the wrong-type refusal landing before claude is spawned, argv-verified empty; the grant list byte-unchanged from what I audited; Req 7's invariant (sprint_lifecycle.py untouched); 169 OK across the three suites and a clean tarball at 0.1.19.

THE AMENDMENT IS COMMITTED. My round-3 hold is resolved — the sprint file's working tree is clean and the amendment lives in history rather than in one directory. That mattered more here than in the two previous times I have held for this reason: this amendment IS the authorization record for the broadest grant this project ships, and a PASS hashing a working-tree copy could have left the durable record showing an authorization that existed nowhere.

================================================================
THE CLAUSE I FLAGGED — CORRECTED, AND CORRECTED PROPERLY
================================================================

I checked each of the four against the code again rather than accepting the correction, since the correction is itself a claim:
  budget cap            — absent from this framework entirely
  loop breakers         — absent from this framework entirely
  timeout               — the only one in the launcher is AUTH_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS, 5 seconds, on the auth
                          probe; there is none on the spawned child
  process-group teardown— sprint 15 shipped child.kill(signal), a single-PID kill, and run-role.js:115
                          says in its own words "signals exactly the one PID it's given — never the
                          process group"
The amendment now states all four accurately, cites the same line numbers, and attributes them where they belong: the consuming orchestrator's driver-side controls, which sprint 15's notes already identified as driver-side and which run-role.js:113 is reasoning about rather than providing.

Three things about how it was corrected are worth recording, because they are the difference between a fix and a record:
  - The original wrong claim is preserved in italics rather than silently replaced. A reader six months
    from now sees what was believed, what was checked, and what replaced it.
  - It names why the clause mattered — "no new capability, AND it adds protections the interactive path
    lacks" is what made the trade read as favourable — rather than treating it as a wording slip.
  - It identifies the error as the same generalisation the amendment opens by correcting: redirect
    confinement widened into write confinement, then a consumer's controls attributed to this
    framework, one paragraph apart. Naming the pattern rather than just the instance is what stops it
    recurring a third time.

THE SURVIVING ARGUMENT IS THE RIGHT ONE AND IT DOES NOT NEED THE CLAUSE. "An interactive session already has every one of these escapes and nobody audits a single Bash call in it. This grant creates no capability that is not already exercised daily; what it removes is the property that someone could interrupt." That is true, checkable against this project's own evidence, and sufficient on its own — the amendment says so explicitly ("the first half needs no second half"), which is the correct conclusion and a harder one to write than adding a compensating claim.

The three bounds it now rests on are stated accurately: git recoverability except uncommitted work and .env; .env's own OS-level protection, correctly identified as the one control in this sprint built for exactly this class of escape; and the operator's explicit declaration about their own property. And the note that the client-repository exclusion in Out of Scope now weighs MORE is the right inference — a grant justified by "the operator is trusting their own machine with their own repository" gets weaker, not stronger, the further it travels from that.

ESCALATION FROM ROUND 2 — CLOSED. I asked for a recorded confirmation from whoever authorised this sprint that they still wanted it on the revised basis, before publication. That is now in the sprint file, on the record, with the basis stated as it actually is rather than as it was argued. Nothing further is outstanding from this gate.

INFORMATIONAL, CARRIED, NONE BLOCKING

1. An empty-string declaration ("") still falls through silently rather than refusing, unlike the other
   wrong-type values. Defensible — a cleared value reads differently from a typo — and not worth a
   round.
2. The residual the amendment now states honestly is real and unbounded by anything technical inside
   the declared directory. That is the accepted position, not a gap I am leaving open, but it is the
   thing to revisit first if this grant is ever proposed for a repository the operator does not own.
3. Carried, unchanged: the CLI-version-drift item (sprint-12 findings record no `claude` version, one
   CONFIRMED entry already expired) — still the strongest-evidenced open item; sprint 17's bare-verb
   allowlist question; the --agents argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 19 will now run clean — the file hash matches the committed file and the tree hash was never affected, since sprint 13's exclusion keeps docs/sprints/ out of it. Then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.19, then `verify-publish 19`.

One thing worth saying once, since this sprint took three rounds and every one of them was about a claim rather than a defect: the code shipped in round 1 and has not changed since. Rounds 2 and 3 were entirely about making the sprint say what is true about it. That is the right ratio for a change that grants this much, and it is the first time in this project that a sprint's argument was corrected twice, by two different roles, without anyone defending the original.

PASS: PASS — round 4 (post-dev-done CI fix). Audited 6abcf00, main checkout. Sprint file re-read fresh; `git diff 55d56ee HEAD -- docs/sprints/2-in-progress/` is empty, so requirements are byte-identical to round 3's. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

The gate worked exactly as designed here and it is worth recording why before the findings: a tree-content change landed after a PASS, /sprint-dev-done had already run, and the hash gate forced this audit rather than letting a modified .env-protection code path ship on round 3's verdict. That is the third time this mechanism has caught a real post-audit change, and the first time it caught one that mattered this much.

================================================================
THE SECOND BUG IS THE IMPORTANT ONE, AND I REPRODUCED IT
================================================================

verifyEnvProtected()'s own probe was `printf x >> <file>`. That is a write. On every headless launch with a declared owned repository, on any platform or filesystem where the immutable flag did not take, the check meant to protect .env was appending a byte to it.

Reproduced directly rather than taking the report:
    old probe, unprotected .env:  exit 0, file MUTATED -- "SECRET=abc" became "SECRET=abc\nx"
    new probe, unprotected .env:  exit 0, file UNCHANGED
    new probe, protected .env:    exit 1 ("Operation not permitted"), file UNCHANGED
    old probe, protected .env:    exit 1
So the fix preserves the protected/unprotected distinction exactly — same exit codes in both states — while writing nothing. `: >> file` keeps the append redirect that carries the permission semantics and drops the payload. That is the minimal correct fix and I could not find a behavioural difference between the two probes other than the write.

THE IMPACT, STATED PRECISELY BECAUSE IT IS WORSE THAN "A STRAY x":
    .env WITH a trailing newline    -> gains a stray line "x". Pollution.
    .env WITHOUT a trailing newline -> the last variable's VALUE is corrupted: SECRET=abc becomes
                                       SECRET=abcx, and it accumulates per launch -- SECRET=abcxxx
                                       after three.
Files without a trailing newline are common. This is silent corruption of a secrets file, repeated on every launch, on the platform where it was most likely to fire — Linux without CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE, which this round establishes is the ordinary case including CI containers. Found while chasing something else, self-reported rather than quietly folded in.

AND THE FIX IS VERIFIED IN THE EXACT SCENARIO WHERE THE BUG FIRED. I ran the full launcher with a no-op chflags on PATH, standing in for a platform where protection cannot take:
    ERROR: Could not verify .env protection for: .../.env. Refusing the broad owned-repository grant
           rather than proceeding with these files unprotected -- [platform/capability explanation]
    claude spawned: 0 argv lines
    .env mutated:   NO      .env content: SECRET=abc
Refusal, not degradation; the child never spawned; and the file is byte-identical afterwards — which is precisely what the old probe violated on this same path. The security property sprint 19 was designed around holds, and now the check no longer damages the thing it checks.

================================================================
THE LINUX CAPABILITY FINDING
================================================================

The cause is correctly identified and the conclusion is the right one: chattr +i needs CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE, which an unprivileged user does not have and which a default container does not grant even to root. The failing and passing cases were both confirmed in real containers, which is the standard this project holds itself to and the reason the previous "expected but unverified" note was correctly not left standing.

The security consequence is stated accurately and I checked it against the code rather than the summary: because runHeadless() already refused rather than degraded when verification fails, the real effect on Linux without the capability is that a repository containing any .env* file cannot use the broad grant at all. A hard refusal, never a silent partial grant. That was the original design and it is why this turned out to be an availability limit rather than a hole — worth saying plainly, since "the .env protection does not work on Linux" would have been the natural and wrong summary.

The fail() message now names the capability, says a container does not grant it by default even to root, and gives three ways forward (run with the capability, drop the declaration for the narrower profile, or protect the files by hand). Read cold, someone hitting this in CI can act on it without knowing anything about this sprint.

I did not independently reproduce the Linux container runs — no Linux environment here — and I am recording that rather than implying otherwise. What I verified independently is the probe behaviour, the refusal path, and that .env is left untouched.

================================================================
TESTS, SCOPE, SUITES
================================================================

The enforcement test now probes for the capability first and skips loudly, naming the likely cause, rather than asserting blindly and failing on any machine without it. That is the right shape: a test that cannot run should say why, not fail as though the code were broken. The strict assertion still runs where the capability exists, so the coverage is not quietly lost — confirmed by the handoff's privileged-container run, which I did not reproduce.

The new real-subprocess test covers exactly the scenario I reproduced above: .env present, protection unable to take, launch refused before claude spawns, .env byte-for-byte unchanged.

Scope: run-role.js and launcher_test.js only, confined to the .env-protection path and its coverage. package.json still 0.1.19 — correctly unchanged, since this is a fix inside an unshipped release rather than a new one.

170 OK (up 1), ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.19 (first install)".

EVERYTHING FROM ROUNDS 1-3 STANDS AND IS NOT RE-DERIVED: the sixteen-input adversarial pass at the validator; the wrong-type refusal landing before spawn; the grant list unchanged; Req 7's invariant (sprint_lifecycle.py untouched — re-checked, still empty); the corrected confinement claim and Master Controller's authorization on the revised basis.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. This changes what the .env protection is on Linux: not a guarantee, but a precondition for the broad
   grant. A downstream project on Linux CI with a .env file will simply never get the broad profile
   unless it arranges the capability. That is the honest behaviour and it is now documented in the
   error, but it is worth Master Controller knowing it is an availability constraint on the feature,
   not a footnote — the motivating case for this sprint was unattended runs, and unattended runs are
   usually containers.
2. Carried, unchanged: the empty-string declaration still falling through silently; the CLI-version
   drift item; sprint 17's bare-verb allowlist question; the --agents argv budget on Windows.

RECOMMENDATION

Re-run /sprint-dev-done 19 — it will now pass against this audited tree — then ship and publish 0.1.19, then `verify-publish 19`.

Worth recording once: this sprint has now been audited four times, and the code changed in three of them. Each change came from someone running the thing rather than reasoning about it — the confinement escapes, the Linux capability, and a probe that was quietly damaging the file it existed to protect. The last one would not have been found by any amount of review; it was found because CI ran on a platform the author did not have.
